prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, Katori and Ye. After the full exchange my reasoning is unchanged and, if anything, sharper. The prize criterion is a discovery or invention with a identifiable origin. The magic-wavelength proposal is a specific idea that removes the lattice light shift on the clock transition while keeping many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and the strontium lattice clock and the later 1e-18 accuracy and stability results are decisive, reproducible measurements, which is the standard I apply to instrument work. Independent laboratories with several species reproduce that performance and intercompare at that level. The credited pair maps onto the concept and the decisive realisation, and Ye's contribution extends beyond the first demonstration into stability and many-body clock physics, as Kroll and Mehlig stress. The chair's summary shows that B007 and B005 are both accepted as excellent science, so the choice rests on maturity and credit. On those two grounds B007 is the more defensible: its main reservation (a pending redefinition of the second) concerns downstream payoff, while B005's reservations concern the mechanism of the phenomenon and a named first experimentalist who cannot be credited. I also take the point that my own move to B007 followed reading others, so I have tested it against the case for B005 below and not relied on the count of supporters. I would want the citation to name the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice, as Johansson and Kroll ask, so that it is clearly separate from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control recognitions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains overlap with the precision-spectroscopy lineage honoured in 2005 and 2012, together with uncredited contributions from Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde, Lisdat and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups, and a redefinition of the second that has not yet happened. In answer to the chair's question on wording, I think a citation anchored on magic-wavelength lattice trapping does separate the invention from combs (a measurement tool) and from single-ion clocks (a different trapping and interrogation scheme). The attribution objection I judge to be real but not disqualifying: the two-name limit leaves out strong contributors in almost any instrument prize, and no member has proposed a better-supported pair or third name. The prospective impact lowers the case somewhat but does not remove it, since the accuracy and reproducibility are already established. If the committee concluded the lineage argument was decisive, I would turn to B005 or B012 rather than to a new candidate.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B005 with MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero, arguing that robust, widely reproduced phenomenology over about eight years suffices even though the pairing mechanism is unsettled, and compares it with high-temperature superconductivity in 1987.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my position and I take it seriously. I agree the correlated insulators and superconducting domes are reproduced by many groups and that a prize need not wait for a settled mechanism. My difficulty is not the mechanism. It is that the 2018 experimental discovery is credited here without its first author, Yuan Cao, and that twist-angle disorder makes it hard to say which features are intrinsic, which matters to me as someone who images such interfaces and knows how sample dependence enters. The 1987 comparison is fair, but there the experimental credit went to the discoverers. Here the three-name limit forces a configuration whose experimental part is incomplete. I would reconsider if the committee were convinced that Jarillo-Herrero alone could stand for the experimental discovery, but I am not, so I stay with B007 and keep B005 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Kroll supports B007 with Katori and Ye, stresses Ye's work beyond the first demonstration, opposes adding a third name, and wants the citation built around magic-wavelength neutral-atom trapping.
responses.response: I agree with Kroll on the two names and on the wording, and I adopt his suggested emphasis in my citation. A third name would mean choosing among Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat without a principled basis in the supplied credited names, and that is the same arbitrary cut I object to in other candidates. I do differ slightly on tone. Kroll weighs the prospective payoff as only mildly weakening, while I regard it as the one point where a reasonable member could wait, because the redefinition decision is outside our control. I do not think it should decide this year, as the measurements are already in hand.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B007 first but stresses that precision metrology has been honoured repeatedly (1997, 2005, 2012) and that Lemonde, Lisdat and Ludlow stand outside the credited pair.
responses.response: That is the honest form of the objection and I share it. Where we should be careful is not to treat it as a decisive count of prior prizes. Laser cooling, combs and ion control each rewarded a different enabling idea, whereas the lattice clock rewards a distinct scheme that combines their results. I also accept that Lindroth's AMO background makes her better placed than I am to judge the priority history of the parallel groups, and I would defer to her if she found a clear priority problem with Katori. Her own conclusion, that the concepts are distinct enough, matches mine.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B025 to B007 but asks whether the pending redefinition of the second makes it a reason to wait, and says a clock prize does not capture the intellectual depth of his own favourite.
responses.response: I do not think waiting for the redefinition is justified. A Nobel Prize for discovery or invention, as I understand the criterion from the committee's own public explanation, is not for lifetime achievement or for downstream adoption, so the redefinition is a consequence and not a condition. Waiting also carries a cost, because the credit picture does not improve with time as more groups join. On B025, I agree with Mehlig that the idea has depth, but I remain doubtful of its distinctness from the 2016 recognition and of the settled order of the transitions, so I would not shift my configuration toward it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes if the citation is not clearly worded around magic-wavelength neutral-atom trapping.
Whether Katori and Ye are the right pair given Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups, which I cannot resolve from the supplied materials.
Whether B005 could be given a fair experimental credit without Yuan Cao, which is the one point that could reverse my ordering of B007 and B005.
Whether a redefinition of the second not yet being decided makes this year premature for a metrology prize.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from my profile for B007 or for the alternatives B005 and B012. My connections (Chalmers colleagues, Japanese academic exchanges, microscopy leadership) do not document links to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Halzen, Karle or Yoshida. Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, so I did not treat his B044 position as independent of institutional context; since B044 is not in my configuration, no recusal is needed.
